introduction: “Moderation is necessary in all things, for if strength exceedeth its bounds it turneth into weakness.” These short readings apply one idea at several scales. In personal life it is evenness under good and bad fortune, a balance of spiritual and material, rest and work in their hours, wisdom in how faith is shown. In society it is a middle between extremes of wealth and enforced equality, and a warning that liberty and civilization themselves become harmful past their measure. In the body it is the equilibrium of elements that is health; in creation, the gradual growth of a tree. Few teachings have wider company. Confucius, the Buddha and Aristotle each made the mean the centre of an ethics; the Qur’án speaks of measure and the Balance; Proverbs and Ecclesiastes counsel sufficiency; Shakespeare puts it in the mouths of Nerissa and Isabella. Two voices dissent from different sides: Blake, for whom excess is the road to wisdom, and Gandhi, who expected an immoderate civilization to destroy itself and saw no reason to save it.
questions: “If strength exceedeth its bounds it turneth into weakness.” Name a strength of yours that becomes a fault when carried too far.
The readings do not “deprecate comfort” and do not let it be the whole of life. Where is the line for you, and how do you know when you have crossed it?
Liberty and civilization are named as goods that turn harmful in excess. Plato said as much of liberty. What present example would you give?
Ecclesiastes says “be not righteous over much.” How do the readings on displays of faith help in understanding that advice?
Blake’s “road of excess” has had many followers. What would the readings say is learned on it, and at what price?

outside.why: “If strength exceedeth its bounds it turneth into weakness.” Confucius, asked which of two disciples was the better: to go beyond is as wrong as to fall short.
Shakespeare’s Isabella on strength that has passed its bounds: it is excellent to have a giant’s strength; but it is tyrannous to use it like a giant.
“For all things there is fixed a station, measure and limit.” The Qur’án: Lo! We have created every thing by measure.
Life depends on “moderation and timely action.” Ecclesiastes: to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
Aristotle makes timing part of the definition of virtue: to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, is not for every one, nor is it easy.
“There should be the perfect balance, the spiritual and the physical.” The Buddha’s first sermon, after years of luxury and years of self-starvation: avoiding both of these extremes, the middle way.
“We do not deprecate comfort. … But man should not think of comfort alone.” Agur’s prayer: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me.

The more people act with moderation, the more capacity they acquire for spirituality. Blake’s proverb of Hell says the reverse: the road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom. Has excess ever taught you something moderation could not, and what did the lesson cost?
“When fate approaches, be not elated, and when it retreats be not saddened.” Kipling: meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same.
Night for rest, day for work: “what God has created has the utmost balance, but man corrupts” it. Nerissa to Portia: they are as sick that surfeit with too much as they that starve with nothing.
“Moderation in all things is desirable,” including in how faith is shown. Paul: let your moderation be known unto all men.

Grand displays of religion stir envy; “it is better to observe moderation.” Ecclesiastes goes so far as to say: be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise. Can one have too much of a virtue, or only too much display of it?
Absolute equality is “just as untenable” as extremes of wealth. Aristotle: the best political community is formed by citizens of the middle class.
The Qur’án on the individual’s side of the same balance: let not thy hand be chained to thy neck nor open it with a complete opening.
“Be temperate, even in the size of the ships you build and in their speed.” Proverbs: hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee.

Liberty and civilization, carried beyond moderation, “cease to exert a beneficial influence.” Plato: the excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery.
Gandhi did not think modern civilization needed moderating: one has only to be patient and it will be self-destroyed. Do the readings ask for less civilization or for a different measure of it?

Health is “the proportionate equilibrium” of the body’s elements. Antony’s praise of Brutus applies the same idea to character: the elements so mix’d in him that Nature might stand up and say to all the world, “This was a man.”
The body is kept by an equilibrium of its elements. Simmias in the Phaedo compares it to a tuned instrument: harmony is a thing invisible, abiding in the lyre which is harmonized.
“The truth lies between the two extremes.” Aristotle’s definition of virtue is built on the same figure: virtue is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean.

A prayer that neither “madness” nor “excessive reason and learning” prevail. Pope’s portrait of the creature who needs it: with too much knowledge for the sceptic side, with too much weakness for the stoic’s pride.
God “suffers a tree to grow a long time,” though He could bring it to fruit in an instant. Jesus: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.

“Whoso cleaveth to justice, can, under no circumstances, transgress the limits of moderation.” The Qur’án joins the two: We revealed the Scripture and the Balance, that mankind may observe right measure.

mark-first-the-blade.text: For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear
